events.text: The Kingdom's Examination of {pw_kingdom} is sat in a barn the size of a church, two hundred candidates on benches. Your candle is the cheap kind and gutters. The farmer's son beside you, Tobin Ash, has two, and is watching yours die.

effects.log: He hands it over without a word. At the end he asks you to read his last answer and you tell him it is good. It is.

choices.text: Write by the light of his

effects.log: You lean so close he complains twice. You finish. So does he, crossly.

events.text: Old Widow Marl teaches the examination for a copper a lesson in her kitchen, between loaves. She failed it herself, she says, because she was a woman in the wrong year. She makes you recite the Kingdom's laws while she kneads.

effects.log: You know every law in {pw_kingdom} and how to make bread, and you are not sure which will be more use.

choices.text: Ask her to sit it with you this year

effects.log: She laughs until she has to sit down. Then she does sit it, and passes, and goes back to her loaves.

events.text: A clerk at the examination office offers to sell you this year's questions for a month's wages. He sells them every year, he says; the Council knows and does nothing, because their own children buy them.

effects.log: You sit it honestly. You hear later that the questions were changed at the last moment, and half the buyers wept.
The examiner thanks you and does nothing. The clerk is moved to a better post.

events.text: The examination falls in harvest week. Your family needs every pair of hands for the barley, and the head of the house has not said a word about it, which is worse than saying something.

choices.text: Help with the harvest first, then walk to the examination

effects.log: Two nights without sleep. You arrive with barley in your hair and an answer in your head.

choices.text: Go, and pay a neighbour to take your place in the field

effects.log: It costs your savings. The old farmer you work for says the neighbour is slower than you, which from him is a compliment.

events.text: A priest of the Maker comes to bless the candidates. He stops at your bench, looks at you oddly, and says, 'You have the hands of someone who made something once.' Then he moves on, as if he had said nothing at all.

effects.log: He frowns and says he does not know; the words came. He gives you his blessing twice, to be safe.
You write well. The words stay with you anyway.

events.text: The essay question: 'Should a king be loved or obeyed?' The examiners are known to favour obedience. Your own answer, if you are honest, is neither.

choices.text: Argue neither, and argue it well

ok.log: One examiner marks you first. Another marks you last. The chief examiner reads it twice and breaks the tie upward.

fail.log: The examiners agree, for once, that you have not answered the question.

effects.log: Safe and well made. You pass the essay and forget it by the evening.

events.text: {cth_rival} is sitting the examination this year too, in a good coat bought for it. Their family has paid for three tutors. They nod at you across the barn as if you were the weather.

effects.log: A small war begins that will last your whole career. It starts politely.
This annoys {cth_rival} more than anything you could have said.

events.text: The results are read out from the steps of the Council house by a herald with a cold. He reads your name wrong. Three people in the crowd turn to look at you anyway, because there is only one person it could be.

effects.log: He corrects it. The crowd cheers, mostly for the herald.

choices.text: Let it go and go home to tell your family

effects.log: By evening someone at home has the name written right, on the kitchen wall.

events.text: Your first task as a clerk of {cth_court}: settle whose turn it is to repair the well in Low Fennick. Both halves of the village have been not repairing it for eleven years and drinking from the river.

choices.text: Go to Low Fennick and repair it with them

effects.log: You spend a day in the well and come out a hero and a mess.

choices.text: Order both halves to pay half

effects.log: Fair. They pay. Nobody thanks you.

events.text: A wool merchant, Hal Dunmore, leaves a ham on your desk with a note hoping his toll will be reviewed favourably. It is a very good ham.

effects.log: He sends back a smaller ham, with an apology. You send that back too. He gives up and respects you.

choices.text: Eat the ham and review him like anyone

effects.log: You review him strictly. He is confused and never sends another ham.

events.text: The tax rolls of the western villages are a mess: whole families listed twice, some not at all, a goat recorded as a householder. Your senior, Clerk Abbot Rennet, says it has always been like this and the Council does not want to know.

effects.log: A summer of walking. The goat is removed. The Council does not thank you, but the villages do.

choices.text: Leave the goat on the rolls

effects.log: The goat pays its taxes, through its owner, for many years.

events.text: Your report on the bridge tolls goes to the Council with {cth_rival}'s name on it. You recognise your own spelling mistakes.

effects.log: You wait. In a year {cth_rival} is asked to explain a passage of it and cannot.
The head clerk sighs and puts your name on it too. You and {cth_rival} are now co-authors and enemies.

events.text: A widow, Agna Thrush, has walked two days to petition the Council about a fence her neighbour moved. The petition queue is three weeks long. She has brought her own bread.

effects.log: You walk back with her and look at the fence. It is clearly moved. The neighbour moves it back, grumbling.

choices.text: Put her at the front of the queue

effects.log: She is heard in a day instead of three weeks. The man behind her complains to your senior.

events.text: The Council house is freezing all winter because the firewood contract went to a councillor's cousin who sends green wood. The clerks write in gloves.

choices.text: Buy your own dry wood for the office

effects.log: The clerks love you. The cousin hears and is offended.

choices.text: Write to the Council about the contract

effects.log: The contract is quietly given to someone else. The cousin knows who did it.

events.text: Your senior clerk, Master Pell, is drunk by noon most days and does good work by evening. The Council has sent an inspector, and the inspector comes at noon.

effects.log: You keep the inspector talking about the records for two hours. Pell sobers up. He never forgets it.
Pell is dismissed. His post is offered to you.

events.text: In a drawer of the Council's record room you find a map of {pw_world} older than any kingdom on it. The coastline is right. The hand that drew it is oddly like your own.

effects.log: You keep it in your room. Some nights you look at it for a long time and cannot say why.
The archivist dates it to before the first king and locks it away, puzzled.

events.text: The Council of {pw_kingdom} is split between the river lords, who want a canal, and the hill lords, who want a road. You have the deciding voice on the treasury committee.

effects.log: The river lords toast you. The hill lords stop inviting you to hunt.
The hill lords toast you. The river lords remember.
A small canal and a narrow road. Everyone is disappointed equally, which is called a compromise.

events.text: {cth_ruler} asks you, after a council, whether the Treasurer is honest. The Treasurer is your friend. He is also not honest.

effects.log: {cth_ruler} thanks you. The Treasurer is replaced. He never speaks to you again.
{cth_ruler} looks at you a long time and does not ask you anything important for a year.

events.text: The southern vales of {pw_kingdom} have had a bad harvest. The royal granary is full. The Council says opening it will make the vales lazy.

effects.log: The vales eat. Nobody becomes lazy. The Council is annoyed to be wrong.
The vales eat, and the treasury does not empty. It is a good, dull answer.

events.text: A list of councillors suspected of disloyalty crosses your desk to be signed. Most are guilty of something. One, old Lord Fennel, is guilty only of having said the king's hat was silly.

choices.text: Strike Fennel and sign the rest

effects.log: Fennel never learns who saved him. He keeps saying hats are silly.
Fennel loses his seat. The hat was silly.

events.text: A great family offers you a marriage alliance with their eldest, Lady Cressida Vane, who is clever and wants to run the treasury herself one day. She has told you so to your face, on the first meeting.

effects.log: An alliance of two ambitious people. The Council is frightened of you both, and rightly.

choices.text: Decline, and recommend her for the treasury

effects.log: She is astonished. Ten years later she runs the treasury, and is your best ally.

events.text: You are to address the full Council on the state of the roads. The roads are bad. The councillors own the toll gates on the bad roads.

choices.text: Tell them plainly, with a joke

ok.log: They laugh, and then, uncomfortably, vote for repairs.

fail.log: The joke falls flat. So does the vote.

choices.text: Present the figures and nothing else

effects.log: The figures are damning. Nobody can argue. Nobody votes either.

events.text: Your old friend from the clerks' office, Tobin Ash, has been sent to the far border for losing a ledger. Visiting him would cost you a week and some favour at court.

effects.log: You bring cheese and news. He laughs and shows you his garden. The court thinks you sentimental.
He writes back for years. He says the garden is doing well.

events.text: Your oath to {cth_throne} forbids you to keep secrets from the crown. An old friend has asked you to keep one: they are in debt, and the creditor is a councillor.

choices.text: Tell the crown, and pay the debt yourself

effects.log: The crown is amused. Your friend is furious, then grateful. The councillor is embarrassed.
You keep it. The oath sits on you like a wet coat.

events.text: An order comes under your oath: close the free market in Wendle so the chartered merchants profit. The order is lawful. The poor of Wendle shop at the free market.

effects.log: The market closes. Your protest is read and filed.
The delay lasts a year. By then the order has been forgotten.

events.text: A young clerk, Mira Hollis, is to swear the oath to the crown and has asked you to stand as her witness. She is very good and very rude.

effects.log: She is rude for ten years and then indispensable.
She is cool to you after, and right to be.

events.text: A colleague, Ser Dunstan Holt, breaks his oath in open Council and walks out to become a beekeeper. The Council is scandalised.

effects.log: He is happy and poor and asks after your oath. You come home with honey and doubts.
You stay. An oath is a promise, and you made it.

events.text: A priest of the Maker asks to hear your oath recited, as is the custom every ten years. When you finish he says, softly, 'The Maker made a promise too, they say, and kept it by leaving us alone.'

effects.log: He does not know. He thinks about it all evening, and so do you.
You go. The words follow you home.

events.text: The anniversary of your oath: by custom you keep a night's vigil in the Council chapel. The candles go out in a draught at midnight. In the dark the old verger begins to sing.

effects.log: It is a song about the first king. It is very long and you are sorry when it ends.
You relight them all. The verger nods and keeps singing.

events.text: A wool baron, Lord Haskel, will pay for the printing of your poems if you put his name in the dedication and his dead hound in a poem.

effects.log: It is the best poem in the book. Haskel weeps. Readers love the hound.
Two hundred copies, slowly sold, each one loved.

events.text: Your ballad is being sung in the taverns of {pw_kingdom}, with the last verse changed by a drover named Kit Barrow. The change is better.

choices.text: Find Kit Barrow and buy him a drink

effects.log: You write a new verse together. The taverns sing that one too.

choices.text: Have it printed with your verse

effects.log: The taverns keep singing his.

events.text: The Council's censor wants a stanza cut from your new book because it laughs at a councillor. It laughs at him fondly.

effects.log: The book is printed with a gap. Readers fill in the gap with something much ruder.
The councillor reads it and laughs. The censor does not.

events.text: A soldier's mother asks you for a poem for her son's funeral. 'Not about glory,' she says. 'He hated glory. He liked onions.'

effects.log: The whole funeral laughs and cries at once. The mother keeps it in her prayer book.
It is a fine poem. She thanks you politely.

events.text: A shepherd boy, Wren, brings you his poems on scraps of bark. They are rough and very good. He asks if he should give up sheep.

effects.log: He keeps both. His sheep poems are famous in a hundred years.

choices.text: Find him a patron in the city

effects.log: He goes to the city and writes clever poems. He misses the sheep.

events.text: You write a long poem about the making of {pw_world}, as the priests tell it. Halfway through, the lines start coming faster than you can write, as if remembered. The ending is not the one the priests tell.

effects.log: The priests are troubled. The people love it. Nobody can say where you heard it.
It is a good, proper poem. You keep the other ending in a drawer.

events.text: Drill with {cth_legion} on a muddy field outside the town. Sergeant Bracken shouts. Half the levy are farmers who have never held a spear, and the other half are farmers who have held one wrong.

choices.text: Help the slowest ones after drill

effects.log: By the end of the month your file is the best in the levy, and they buy you dumplings.

choices.text: Drill hard and keep your head down

effects.log: You are good. The sergeant notices.

events.text: A boy of the levy, Penn Archer, is caught slipping home at night. His mother is ill and nobody gave him leave. The penalty is a flogging.

choices.text: Speak for him to the captain

effects.log: The captain gives him three days and you his watches. He comes back.
He takes it. He serves well after, and never speaks to you.

events.text: The levy's boots were bought from the cheapest bidder and fall apart in the rain. The quartermaster says there is no more money. The march is next week.

choices.text: Pay the cobbler in town to resole your file's boots

effects.log: It costs you a month of pay. Your file arrives dry-footed and grateful.
The captain complains to the Council. New boots arrive after the march.

events.text: Your file has a marching song about the captain's nose. It is very catchy. The captain has heard it.

effects.log: The captain hears the new verse and laughs. The song is sung for generations.
They sing it everywhere you are not.

events.text: Night watch on the border hill. Your watch partner, old Gaffer Thorne, has fallen asleep. There are lights moving in the valley below.

choices.text: Wake him and signal the camp

effects.log: It is a smugglers' train. The camp catches them and their brandy.

ok.log: It is a lost wedding party with lanterns. You guide them to the road. They give you cake.

fail.log: You fall in a ditch and twist your ankle. It was a wedding party.

events.text: Half your file cannot write, and the levy's scribe is ill. They line up with letters for mothers and sweethearts and one for a dog.

effects.log: Forty letters. You know your file now better than their mothers do.
A winter of lessons. Some write you letters years later, misspelled.

events.text: You are offered command of your file in {cth_legion}. The old file leader, Ned Copper, is being put aside because his knees are going. He taught you to hold a spear.

choices.text: Accept and keep him as your second

effects.log: He grumbles and stays. Your file is the best in the levy.

choices.text: Decline while he can still stand

effects.log: The captain thinks you odd. Ned buys you a cup of tea and tells you never to do that again.

events.text: A lord's son has joined the levy for the glory and brought a servant to carry his spear. The servant, a small, tough girl called Tansy, is the best soldier in the camp.

choices.text: Have Tansy enrolled in her own right

effects.log: The lord's son is offended. Tansy is a sergeant in a year.
Tansy carries the spear. The lord's son gets the medal.

events.text: You command the levy of a whole vale, and the supply carts are stuck behind a flooded ford. Your quartermaster, Mistress Hobb, says the miller upstream could open his sluices and drain it, for a price.

effects.log: The ford drains. The supplies arrive. The miller is rich.

choices.text: Order him to open the sluice

effects.log: He opens it, sullenly. He will sell you nothing again.

events.text: An order from the Council tells you to attack the enemy's hill fort at dawn. Your scouts say the enemy has doubled the garrison. The order is a week old.

effects.log: The Council cancels it a day later. You saved the levy and got a reprimand for slowness.
You take the fort at great cost. The Council is delighted.

events.text: You have taken a hundred prisoners and have no food for them. The nearest town is three days off.

effects.log: Most keep it. The enemy hears of it, and your name is said differently on the other side.

choices.text: March them to town on half rations

effects.log: Three hungry days for everyone. They arrive.

events.text: A spy is caught in your camp: a laundress who has been sending the enemy your laundry lists. She says they paid well and her children are hungry.

choices.text: Send her back with false lists

effects.log: The enemy spends a month puzzling over shirts. She comes back to work for you.

choices.text: Hand her to the captain's court

effects.log: She is sent to the stocks for a week. Her children are fed by the camp.

events.text: A council of war. Every commander wants the cavalry. The marshal, an old woman called Dame Ottilie, likes short speeches.

choices.text: Make your case in a sentence

ok.log: "Give them to me and I will bring you their banner." The cavalry is yours.

fail.log: Too clever. The cavalry goes to someone with three sentences.

choices.text: Give way to a commander who needs them more

effects.log: She wins her battle and remembers you.

events.text: Winter closes the passes. Your army is stuck in a mountain valley until spring, with not enough firewood.

choices.text: Ration the wood and share your tent

effects.log: A cold, close winter. Everyone lives. Everyone remembers your snoring.
Warm, and stranded until wheelwrights come.

events.text: The harvest in {cth_fief} is thin. Your steward, old Amos Pike, says the people can pay the tithe to the crown, but it will hurt.

choices.text: Pay part of it from your own purse

effects.log: Your purse is light. The vale remembers.
Paid on time, in silence.

events.text: The mill in {cth_fief} is owned by a family that charges a third of every sack to grind it. It is legal. It is also why the vale is poor.

effects.log: It costs a year of rents. The price of milling halves. The old family hates you.
Expensive. The family takes the money and moves to the city.

events.text: There is no school in {cth_fief}. A retired priest teaches letters in the porch of the chapel, when it is not raining.

effects.log: In twenty years three of those children sit the Kingdom's Examination.

choices.text: Pay the priest and buy a roof for the porch

effects.log: Cheap and kind. He teaches until he is too old, then teaches his successor.

events.text: Two families of {cth_fief}, the Cobbs and the Greaves, have been feuding over a boundary stone for three generations. Someone moved it again last night.

choices.text: Have a new stone cut with both names on it

effects.log: They grumble. The feud fades, slowly, into a friendly rivalry about pigs.
The Cobbs win. The Greaves leave the vale.

events.text: Wolves have been taking sheep in the high pastures of {cth_fief}. The shepherds want a hunt. The priest says the wolves were here first.

effects.log: Expensive. The wolves go hungry and move on. Nobody hunts anything.

ok.log: You drive the pack over the ridge into the next lordship. The shepherds cheer.

fail.log: You come back cold, bitten and with no wolves.

events.text: {cth_fief} holds a fair every summer, and by custom the lord opens it by eating the first pie. Your predecessor refused. The baker, Mother Juniper, has made a pie the size of a cartwheel.

choices.text: Eat the pie, as much as you can

effects.log: You eat a great deal of pie. The vale stops calling you the new lord.

choices.text: Cut it and share it out

effects.log: Proper and generous. Mother Juniper is a little hurt.

events.text: A widow of {cth_fief}, Hester Lark, has petitioned you: her husband's brother claims her farm under an old law. The law is clear and unjust.

effects.log: You search the chapel records and find one: the farm goes to whoever ploughed it. Hester keeps it.
The brother takes it. Hester leaves the vale.

events.text: The road out of {cth_fief} floods every spring and cuts the vale off from the market. A causeway would cost five years of rents.

effects.log: Five lean years. Then the vale sells its wool all year and grows rich.
Cheap. The ferryman becomes the most important person in the vale.

events.text: The College of Heralds asks what your arms will be. Old families have lions and towers. The herald suggests a sheaf of barley, tactfully.

effects.log: A plain sheaf. Some lords sneer. Farmers like it.
The heralds wince. Clerks across {pw_kingdom} adopt it as a badge.

events.text: The great lords of {pw_kingdom} hunt together every autumn, and the newest lord must ride in front and open every gate. You have never been on a horse for longer than an hour.

ok.log: You open every gate and fall off only once, into a hedge, gracefully. The lords decide you will do.

fail.log: You fall off at the first gate. They talk about it for a year.

choices.text: Walk, and open the gates on foot

effects.log: The lords are baffled, then amused. You arrive last and on time.

events.text: Your title obliges you to send soldiers to {cth_legion} in war. Your household is a cook, two grooms and an elderly steward.

effects.log: The levy is satisfied. Your purse is not.
A lord in the ranks. The soldiers think you mad and like you for it.

events.text: A ruined old family, the Ashcombes, is selling its manor to pay its debts. The last Ashcombe, a proud, threadbare old woman, will have to move to a cottage.

choices.text: Buy it and let her stay

effects.log: She is furious and grateful. When she dies she leaves you her family's letters, which are extraordinary.

choices.text: Let it go to the highest bidder

effects.log: A brewer buys it. She writes rude letters to everyone.

events.text: An old family proposes that their heir marry into your house, to join your new title to their old name and their old debts.

effects.log: Doors open. So do your coffers.
They are relieved; they had a better offer.

events.text: Your hall has no family portraits. Visiting lords look at the bare walls and say nothing very loudly.

choices.text: Hang portraits of the farmers who raised you

effects.log: Plain faces. Some lords find it vulgar. You find it right.

choices.text: Buy some old portraits at auction

effects.log: You now have a great-grandfather nobody knows. He looks very proper.

events.text: The regency council of {pw_kingdom} has seven members, each of whom thinks the regency should have been theirs. Today they are deadlocked on raising the salt tax.

choices.text: Break the tie for the poor

effects.log: The tax stays low. The council sulks. The towns hear of it.
The treasury fills. The towns grumble.

events.text: The palace food taster, Old Simkin, has tasted for two regents before you. He says the last one was poisoned slowly, through the pear brandy. He thinks you should stop serving the pear brandy at your table.

effects.log: The brandy is traced to a merchant paid by a councillor. The councillor is removed.

choices.text: Keep it on the table, untouched, and watch who watches it

effects.log: One councillor always looks away. You send him to govern a very small island.

events.text: The new coins show the regent's face beside the crown. The mint master says it is customary.

effects.log: The coins show only the crown. The people think you modest.
Your face is in every purse. People begin to think of the crown as yours.

events.text: A rumour runs through the taverns that you will never give up the regency. It is not true. It is very widely believed.

choices.text: Announce the date of the handover

effects.log: A date settles the taverns.
The rumour grows fat on silence.

events.text: General Harrow asks the regency to approve a war against a weak neighbour. It would unite the kingdom behind you. He is probably right.

effects.log: No war. The kingdom stays divided, and you sleep.
A border town is taken. The kingdom cheers. A family in the town moves out.

events.text: The court physician, Doctor Elsworth, says the regency is aging you faster than war would. He prescribes a garden and a month.

effects.log: The kingdom does not fall in a month. You come back slower and wiser.
There is always too much to do.

events.text: The first petitioner in the King's Hall today is a farmer who has walked a week to complain about a tax collector. The tax collector is here too, with a lawyer.

effects.log: You rule for the farmer. The whole kingdom hears that you did.
Proper. The farmer walks home a week.

events.text: The vales send their gifts to the crown at midsummer: wool, cheese, a white horse, and from the poorest vale, a jar of pickled onions and a letter of apology.

choices.text: Thank the onion vale in open hall

effects.log: The hall laughs and then, seeing your face, stops. The onion vale names a fair after you.
The treasury fills. The horse bites a councillor.

events.text: A thief, Jem Rook, stole grain from the royal granary in the famine to feed his village. The law says ten years in the salt mines. The village has sent a petition with six hundred marks on it.

choices.text: Pardon him and change the law

effects.log: A long argument with the Council. The law changes. Jem Rook becomes the granary keeper.
He serves a year on the roads. The kingdom thinks you firm but fair.

events.text: Your chancellor, Lord Pomfret, agrees with everything you say, even the things you say to test him.

choices.text: Move him to a post where he must say no

effects.log: He is miserable and, surprisingly, good at it.
You hear only good news, until the day you do not.

events.text: You could go to the market in plain clothes, as the old kings did in stories, to hear what people really say. Your guard captain, Dame Hollis, is firmly against it.

choices.text: Go, with Dame Hollis in plain clothes too

effects.log: You hear a very rude song about yourself. Dame Hollis laughs, then denies it.
You get an accurate report with no song in it.

events.text: A child has slipped past the guards into the King's Hall during audience and is asking, loudly, for a lost cat.

choices.text: Send the guards to find the cat

effects.log: The cat is in the royal kitchens. The story is told for a hundred years.

choices.text: Have the child taken out gently

effects.log: Correct. The child cries all the way home.

events.text: The Master of Works wants to build a statue of you over the city gate. It would take a thousand masons five years.

effects.log: A long, useful bridge, named for nobody.
It is magnificent. Pigeons love it.

events.text: The Council asks you to name an heir to {cth_throne}. The candidates are a capable general, a gentle chancellor and a sharp young judge who reminds you of yourself.

effects.log: The kingdom sighs with relief.
The court is startled. The judge does not sleep for a week, then gets to work.
The court keeps guessing.

events.text: The Rising of the Vale needs a banner. Old Nell Weaver will sew it for nothing, if you swear her village will pay no tax for ten years after you win.

effects.log: She sews the finest banner the vale has seen. You have made your first promise as a leader.
She takes the money. The banner is good, not great.

events.text: Volunteers come every night to the rising's camp in the woods: farmers, out-of-work weavers, a few deserters from {cth_legion}. Your quartermaster says there is not food for all of them.

effects.log: A hungry army is still an army.

choices.text: Take only those who can fight

effects.log: A lean army. The others go home and talk.

events.text: A letter from {cth_ruler}: amnesty for every one of your followers, if you alone surrender and go into exile.

choices.text: Read it to your followers and refuse

effects.log: They cheer. Nobody deserts.
Someone finds out. Trust drops.

events.text: The rising has taken its first town. The crown's bailiffs are still there, three terrified men with ledgers. Your followers want to make an example of them.

choices.text: Send them home with their ledgers

effects.log: They tell the court you are reasonable. The court is more frightened by that than anything.

choices.text: Lock them in the tithe barn

effects.log: Safe, and a little cruel.

events.text: There is a spy in the camp. Your lieutenant, Corwin Thatch, thinks it is the cook, who makes the best stew in the vale.

choices.text: Test the cook with a false plan

effects.log: The cook was the spy. She weeps. You send her home.

choices.text: Trust the cook and look elsewhere

effects.log: The spy was Corwin Thatch. The stew goes on.

events.text: A priest of the Maker comes to the camp and blesses the banner. 'The Maker does not take sides,' she says. 'But I think the Maker would like to see what you do with this.'

choices.text: Ask her what the Maker would do

effects.log: "Leave," she says. "And trust us to manage." You think about that a long time.
You march. The blessing stays with the banner.

events.text: A young clerk of {cth_court} walks all day to ask your advice on a petition. You have no power now. That, she says, is why she came.

effects.log: She goes away with a plan, and you feel twenty years younger.

choices.text: Send her back with a note

effects.log: The note is short and wise. She keeps it on her desk.

events.text: A printer wants your memoirs. Half the Council has sent you gifts with notes hoping your memory is failing.

effects.log: It is kind and it still ends two careers.
A book about leeks. The Council buys every copy, relieved.

events.text: Your old rival {cth_rival} has retired to the next village. They have sent over a bottle of plum brandy and no note.

effects.log: Bottles go back and forth for years. Neither of you writes a word.

choices.text: Walk over and share a pot of tea with them

effects.log: A long, strange evening. You argue about everything and laugh at most of it.

events.text: A girl from the village, Pip, wants you to teach her letters so she can sit the Kingdom's Examination one day.

effects.log: She is slow and stubborn and wonderful. Years later she passes, and sends you a cheese.
She passes sooner, and never knows who paid.

events.text: The river floods your village. Your old house, from your days of power, stands on the only high ground.

choices.text: Open it to the whole village

effects.log: A hundred people in your house for three days. You have never been happier.

choices.text: Open it to the children and the old

effects.log: They are safe. The rest go to the chapel.

events.text: You dream, more often now, of a sky without stars and your own two hands setting them out one by one. The village priest, when you tell him, goes quiet and asks you to describe the first star.

effects.log: He writes it down carefully. On the next holy day he preaches about the first star, and gets it exactly right.
He laughs too, a little too late.

events.text: {cth_Realm} is at war with {cth_foe}. The levy has come from {cth_throne}: every lordship must send men and women and carts. Your quota is twice what the vale can spare.

effects.log: The quota is met. The vale is short of hands at harvest.

fail.log: The Council doubles it for insolence.

events.text: Refugees from {cth_foe} have crossed the border river: four hundred of them, old and young, with handcarts. The border captain wants to send them back.

effects.log: In ten years they are the best cheesemakers in the kingdom.

choices.text: Feed them and send them on

effects.log: They go, fed. Some write, years later.

events.text: Your levy, {cth_legion}, has taken a market town of {cth_foe}. Its people never chose the war. The Council asks whether it should be made part of {cth_realm}.

choices.text: Annex it gently, keeping its laws and fairs

effects.log: It grumbles and then settles.
It is quiet, and in twenty years it rebels.

events.text: A letter arrives from a scholar of {cth_foe} you wrote to before the war. It is about poetry. Read carefully, it is about peace.

effects.log: A year of poems, then peace, then you show it to {cth_ruler}.
The Council calls it treason. The scholar does not write again.

events.text: A girl of the levy, Bel Fairweather, held a bridge alone for a night. The Council wants a hero for the posters. Bel wants to go home to her goats.

choices.text: Give her a medal and send her home

effects.log: She is the pride of her village forever, and her goats do not care.

choices.text: Make her the face of the war

effects.log: Her face is everywhere. She is very unhappy.

events.text: The war's dead are brought home in carts to the capital. Somebody must read the names in the square. There are nine hundred names.

effects.log: It takes a day. Your voice goes. The kingdom never forgets it.
Proper and correct.

events.text: A footbridge across the border river still stands, and at night soldiers of both sides meet on it to swap tobacco and news. Your orders are to burn it.

effects.log: It burns. Both banks are quiet that night.
A month of trade. Someone on both sides starts talking about peace.

events.text: An offer of peace comes from {cth_foe}: two towns back for one, and nobody admits anything. The war party on the Council says to press for more.

effects.log: Peace, with nothing admitted. The war party calls you soft.
One more town, and nine hundred more names.

events.text: Your envoy to {cth_foe}, a careful man called Osric Venn, sends his first report: nine pages about the food and one line about their cavalry.

effects.log: You find the cavalry line, and another about a quarrel in their council.
His next report is one line. It is about the food.

events.text: Your envoy writes that the court of {cth_foe} expects a gift. She asks whether she may give them the silver pen you gave her when she left.

effects.log: The pen is a triumph. Her new one arrives a month later.

choices.text: Send a proper gift from the treasury

effects.log: Grand, and late.

events.text: Your envoy has been arrested in the court of {cth_foe} for spying. He was buying their cheese, in very large amounts, for you.

effects.log: He is released, red-faced. The cheese is excellent.
He is released, coldly. The cheese comes anyway.

events.text: You must choose an envoy for {cth_foe}: Lady Thessaly, brilliant and proud; Clerk Bunce, humble and dull; or a wandering pedlar, Jory Quill, who speaks their dialect and has no family name worth mentioning.

effects.log: The Council is scandalised. Jory is perfect.
She comes home with a treaty and three enemies.
He is dull, and they trust him for it.

events.text: Your envoy comes home after ten years in the court of {cth_foe}, dressing like them and defending them at dinner.

choices.text: Make her your advisor on them

effects.log: She is invaluable, and the Council distrusts her forever.
You lose the only person who understood them.

events.text: Your envoy has made a good treaty with {cth_foe}. It gives away one village nobody on the Council has ever visited. Three hundred people live there and were not asked.

choices.text: Sign, and send someone to ask the village

effects.log: Half want to stay. You pay for the others to move.
The village hears of it from a herald.

events.text: A boy of fifteen named Davey Moss has lied about his age to join {cth_legion}. You can see it in his wrists. His older sister Ada has followed him to the camp and is standing at the gate, refusing to leave until he comes home. The sergeant wants one of them gone by morning, and he does not mind which.

choices.text: Send Davey home with his sister

effects.log: Davey cries with rage all the way down the road. Ada looks back once and nods.

choices.text: Keep Davey, and make him your runner

effects.log: Ada leaves him in your charge. "If he comes back hurt," she says, and does not finish.
The sergeant laughs and does it. Ada is a far better soldier than her brother.

events.text: The levy marches to the border. On the third night the camp is raided, and in the dark you lose track of the boy. At dawn there is no sign of Davey Moss, only his cap by the stream and a trail of small footprints going the wrong way, towards {cth_foe}.

ok.log: You find him at noon in a hayloft, hiding from both armies. You bring him back.

fail.log: You lose the trail in the river. He comes back by himself a week later, thin and silent.

choices.text: Report him missing and march on

effects.log: Orders are orders. He turns up a week later, half starved, with a story nobody believes.

events.text: Davey Moss has grown. He is a sergeant now, with a voice like his old sergeant's, and he has a recruit of his own who has lied about her age: a girl called Meg, all wrists. Davey comes to you to ask what to do with her, and he looks very embarrassed about it.

choices.text: Ask him what he wishes someone had done for him

effects.log: He thinks for a long time and sends Meg home, with a letter for her mother and his own boots.

choices.text: Tell him it is his decision now

effects.log: He makes it. You never ask which way, and he never tells you.

events.text: Ada Moss writes to you. She has a farm now, and children, and her brother Davey is home at last, with a bad knee and a medal. 'You sent him back to me once when he was a fool,' she writes. 'I have never thanked you. Come at harvest. There will be too much pie.'

effects.log: There is far too much pie. Davey tells the story of the hayloft wrong and you let him.

choices.text: Write back and send a gift

effects.log: You send seed corn. She sends back a pie by carrier. It arrives in pieces and is wonderful.

events.text: You are named regent of {pw_kingdom} for a king of six named Alder, who likes frogs and is frightened of the crown, which is too big for him and slides over his eyes. His nurse, Goody Wren, holds his hand. His uncle, Lord Mortlake, who expected the regency himself, bows very low to you.

choices.text: Promise Alder, in front of the court, to give the crown back

effects.log: Alder nods and asks if he can keep the frogs. You say yes. The court writes it down.
The goldsmith grumbles and makes a small crown. Alder wears it every day after, even to bed.

events.text: Lord Mortlake proposes, kindly, that the boy be sent to his own castle in the north for safety until he comes of age. Half the regency council agrees. Goody Wren catches your sleeve in a corridor. 'If Alder goes north,' she says, 'he will not come back.'

choices.text: Refuse, and keep the boy at court

effects.log: Mortlake withdraws the proposal and keeps his smile.

choices.text: Send Mortlake north instead, with honours

ok.log: He is made Warden of the North and cannot refuse. The council is relieved.

fail.log: The council splits, and Mortlake knows your mind now.

choices.text: Agree, and send Goody Wren with him

effects.log: Alder goes north. Goody Wren's letters grow shorter every month.

events.text: A royal decree appears in Alder's careful round hand, naming Lord Mortlake sole regent. Alder, shown it, bursts into tears and says he never wrote it. Goody Wren says the boy spent an afternoon last month practising his letters with his uncle.

effects.log: Mortlake is stripped of his lands. The kingdom trusts the regency more.

choices.text: Let Alder decide his uncle's fate

effects.log: Alder thinks hard and says: send him somewhere with no ink. The court laughs and remembers.

events.text: Alder is grown: tall and shy, and still fond of frogs. The day comes to hand back {cth_throne}. The regent's seal is heavy in your hand. Goody Wren, very old now, is in the front row, already crying.

choices.text: Hand it over and step down

effects.log: You hand it over. The kingdom sees a regent who kept the promise. Alder does not let you go far.

choices.text: Hand it over and stay as advisor

effects.log: Alder asks you to stay. You stay, and he learns to rule with you at his shoulder.
He agrees, coolly. Neither of you forgets it.

events.text: Goody Wren is gone, peacefully. King Alder asks you to speak at her funeral, because you kept him at court when it mattered. The whole palace comes, and the frog pond is full of lilies she planted.

choices.text: Speak about the day she caught your sleeve

effects.log: Alder hears for the first time how close it was. He holds your arm through the rest of it.

choices.text: Let Alder speak, and stand by him

effects.log: He speaks, and stumbles, and finishes. You stand at his shoulder.

events.text: The High Priestess of the Maker, Mother Isolde, asks the crown for money to build a great hall to the Maker in the capital. 'Nobody has seen the Maker,' she admits. 'We are not sure the Maker would want it. But the people want somewhere to say thank you.' The Treasurer is against it. So is the Council.

effects.log: A plain hall of grey stone, with a door that is never locked.
A great hall with a gold roof. The people love it. The treasury groans.
Mother Isolde bows and says she thought you might. She does not seem surprised.

events.text: A child of the city, a ragged, sharp-eyed girl called Linnet, has been telling everyone she has seen the Maker in a dream, and that the Maker looks exactly like you. The priests are troubled. The Council is amused. The crowd at your gate is neither.

choices.text: Have the child brought to you

effects.log: She looks at you for a long time and says, "No. The Maker was sadder." Then she asks for a bun. You give her two.

choices.text: Have it announced that the crown is not the Maker

effects.log: The announcement only makes more people wonder why it had to be said.
The rumour fades, slowly, like a dream does.

events.text: A drought in {pw_kingdom}. The people crowd the temples asking the Maker for rain. Mother Isolde comes to you, tired. 'They pray and nothing comes,' she says. 'They think the Maker has forgotten them. What should I tell them?'

choices.text: Tell her: the Maker trusted them to manage

effects.log: She looks at you oddly, as if you had quoted something. The next day she preaches it, and the people dig wells.

choices.text: Open the royal reservoirs to the city

effects.log: The crown does what the Maker does not. The people bless you and forget the temples for a while.

choices.text: Tell her you do not know

effects.log: "Nor do I," she says, and you sit together for an hour in silence, which helps them both, a little.

events.text: Mother Isolde is old now. She asks you to walk with her through the Maker's Hall at night, when it is empty. At the far end, where there is no statue, she stops. 'I have spent my life speaking to someone who never answered,' she says. 'And yet, lately, I think they were listening. Do you ever feel that?'

effects.log: She smiles and says nothing more. When she dies, she leaves you the key to the hall that is never locked.

choices.text: Tell her you do not know what you feel

effects.log: "That is how it begins," she says, and pats your hand.
